There is a particular kind of quiet that lives in old maps. It isn't the silence of an empty room but the hush of a page that has been folded and unfolded so many times its creases have gone soft as cloth. I'm drawn to the ones from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, when cartographers filled their margins with sea monsters, compass roses curling like flowers, and little notes admitting what they did not know.

Those admissions fascinate me most. Off the coast of some unexplored continent, a mapmaker might have written "here be dragons" or simply left the land bare. Blank spaces weren't failures. They were honest. They acknowledged that the world was larger than anyone had seen and that understanding it would take patience, ships, and a great many mistakes.

I think about this more than I expected to. We live in an era when every street corner can be pinned, measured, and reviewed by strangers. Nothing seems unmapped anymore, and I suspect we've lost something along with the blank space. A map with gaps invites you to wonder. It asks you to imagine what might be there and then go look.

Maybe that's why I love the old ones. Their errors are charming, their monsters whimsical, and their emptiness a kind of invitation. They remind me that not knowing is not the same as having nothing left to discover.

If I could own one, I'd choose a map with a large, unlabeled region right in the middle. I'd hang it above a desk and let it stay unfinished, the way a good question does. Every so often I'd look at it and remember that the most interesting places are often the ones nobody has written down yet.
